subject: Mathematics
source: Drive: Maths folder, Year 7 Maths LTP (Autumn sequence: factors and multiples, sequences, perimeter and area, negative numbers) and SOW Maths (Year 7 scheme); aligned to the National Curriculum KS3 and Edexcel GCSE (9-1) foundation/higher content

lessons.title: Factors and highest common factor
objectives: List all factors of a number systematically
Find the highest common factor (HCF) of two numbers

keywords.def: a whole number that divides exactly into another number
a factor shared by two or more numbers
the largest number that is a factor of two or more numbers
can be divided exactly with no remainder

starter: Say Bismillah and settle. Work out 7 x 8 and 63 ÷ 9.
List the factors of 12.
Is 91 a multiple of 7? Explain how you know.

teach.heading: Finding all the factors
bullets: Test 1, 2, 3, ... in order and write factor pairs.
teach.note: Stress systematic working: it is the only way to be sure no factor is missed. Ask pupils to say how they know they have finished (the next number up has already appeared as a partner). The factors of 48 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48.

teach.heading: Divisibility tests
bullets: By 3: the digit sum is divisible by 3.
By 4: the last two digits are divisible by 4.
By 9: the digit sum is divisible by 9.
teach.note: Test 756: 7 + 5 + 6 = 18, so divisible by 3 and 9; 56 ÷ 4 = 14, so divisible by 4. 756 ÷ 9 = 84. Remind pupils of 2, 5 and 10 from primary and add 6 (divisible by 2 and 3).

teach.heading: Common factors
teach.note: Write the two lists one above the other and circle the matches. The highest common factor of 48 and 60 is 12. Draw a Venn diagram to show the shared factors in the overlap.

teach.heading: HCF in context
bullets: 48 dates and 60 figs go into identical bags.
No fruit left over: the most bags is HCF = 12.
Each bag has 4 dates and 5 figs.
teach.note: Check: 48 ÷ 12 = 4 and 60 ÷ 12 = 5. Link to sharing food parcels fairly, a Ramadan-style charity project. Ask: why can there not be 24 bags?

practice: List all the factors of 36.
Find the HCF of 24 and 40.
Is 4,248 divisible by 9? Show your test.
independent: List all factors of 54, 72 and 100.
Find the HCF of: 18 and 30; 36 and 54; 45 and 75.
A teacher has 72 pencils and 90 rubbers to share into identical packs. What is the greatest number of packs? What is in each?
Without dividing, decide which of 3,126; 4,572; 8,019 are divisible by 3 and which by 9.
exit: Find the HCF of 28 and 42.
Explain how to test whether 5,274 is divisible by 9.
lessons.homework: Choose three numbers under 100. List all their factors and find the HCF of each pair.
lessons.send: SEND: multiplication grid and factor-pair arrays. EAL: pre-teach factor/divisible/common. Stretch: find the HCF of three numbers.

lessons.title: Multiples and lowest common multiple
objectives: List multiples and recognise common multiples
Find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of two numbers

keywords.def: a number in the times table of another number
a multiple shared by two or more numbers
the smallest number that is a multiple of two or more numbers

starter: Say Bismillah. List the first six multiples of 7.
Find the HCF of 24 and 36.
Is 150 a multiple of 12? Explain.

teach.heading: Listing multiples
teach.note: Common mistake: confusing multiples with factors. A multiple is at least as big as the number; a factor is no bigger. Use the memory aid: Multiples are Many and get bigger, factors are Few and Fit inside.

teach.heading: A bigger LCM
teach.note: Ask: could 72 also be a common multiple? Yes, but it is not the lowest. All common multiples are multiples of the LCM: 36, 72, 108.

teach.heading: Repeating patterns
bullets: A light flashes every 12 s and another every 20 s.
They flash together every LCM seconds.
teach.note: Check: 12 x 5 = 60 and 20 x 3 = 60. Context: two alarms, two buses or two rotas. Ask pupils to invent their own.

teach.heading: Choosing HCF or LCM
bullets: Splitting into equal groups usually means HCF.
Events lining up again usually means LCM.
teach.note: Give two short problems and ask the class to vote HCF or LCM before solving: 'two buses leave together then every 15 and 25 minutes' (LCM 75 min) and 'share 30 and 45 sweets into equal bags' (HCF 15).

practice: Find the LCM of 4 and 10.
Find the LCM of 9 and 12.
Buses leave a stop every 15 and 25 minutes. They leave together at 8:00 am. When do they next leave together?
independent: Find the LCM of: 5 and 7; 8 and 12; 14 and 21.
Two lights flash every 18 s and 30 s. After how many seconds do they flash together?
Pens come in packs of 8 and pads in packs of 6. What is the smallest number of each so that the numbers are equal?
State whether each is HCF or LCM, then solve: 40 and 60 stickers shared into equal packs; two planets line up every 4 and 6 years.
exit: Find the LCM of 6 and 15.
Find the HCF of 18 and 24.
lessons.homework: Make up two word problems, one needing HCF and one needing LCM. Solve them both.
lessons.send: SEND: multiples highlighted on a number grid. EAL: pre-teach multiple/factor/common. Stretch: LCM of three numbers.

lessons.title: Prime numbers and prime factor decomposition
objectives: Recognise primes and write a number as a product of its prime factors
Use index notation for repeated prime factors

keywords.def: a number with exactly two factors: 1 and itself
a factor that is also a prime number
the small number showing how many times a number is multiplied by itself
a diagram that splits a number into smaller factors

starter: Say Bismillah. List the prime numbers below 30.
Work out 2 x 2 x 3 x 5.
Is 91 prime? Test it.

teach.heading: Primes
bullets: A prime has exactly two factors.
1 is not prime. 2 is the only even prime.
teach.note: Test a number by dividing by primes up to its square root. Is 91 prime? 91 = 7 x 13, so no. Is 97 prime? Not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7, so yes.

teach.heading: Factor trees
bullets: Keep splitting until every branch is prime.
Order the primes smallest to largest.
teach.note: Build the tree live. Reassure pupils that different first splits (6 x 10, 4 x 15) lead to the same final primes. This is the fundamental theorem of arithmetic in simple form.

teach.heading: Index notation
teach.note: Check each by multiplying back: 4 x 3 x 5 = 60; 4 x 3 x 7 = 84; 4 x 9 x 5 = 180. The index tells us how many times the prime appears.

teach.heading: Repeated division
bullets: Divide by the smallest prime that works.
teach.note: Show the ladder method alongside the tree. Ask which method pupils prefer and why.

practice: Write 36 as a product of prime factors, using indices.
Write 90 as a product of prime factors.
Is 87 prime? Explain.
independent: Write as products of prime factors: 48; 72; 150; 252.
Which number is 2³ x 3 x 5? Which is 2 x 3² x 7?
Explain why 1 is not a prime number.
exit: Write 56 as a product of prime factors.
Is 57 prime? Explain.
lessons.homework: Make a prime factor tree for each of 40, 63, 100 and 198, and write each using index notation.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn factor trees to complete, prime list card. EAL: pre-teach product/index. Stretch: explain why every number has only one prime factor decomposition.

lessons.title: HCF and LCM using prime factors
objectives: Find HCF and LCM from prime factor decompositions
Use Venn diagrams to organise prime factors

keywords.def: writing a number as a product of primes
a diagram of overlapping circles showing what is shared
highest common factor
lowest common multiple

starter: Say Bismillah. Write 24 as a product of prime factors.
Find the HCF of 12 and 18 by listing factors.
Work out 2² x 3² x 5.

teach.heading: Decompose both numbers
teach.note: Recall the work from last lesson. Write the two decompositions one below the other, aligning the primes in columns.

teach.heading: HCF: the shared primes
bullets: Take the smaller index of each shared prime.
teach.note: Check: 12 divides 60 five times and 84 seven times. Venn diagram: shared primes in the overlap (2, 2, 3); 5 only in 60's circle; 7 only in 84's.

teach.heading: LCM: all the primes
bullets: Take every prime, with the larger index.
teach.note: In the Venn diagram, LCM is the product of every number in both circles, with the overlap counted once. Confirm 420 is a multiple of both.

teach.heading: Bigger indices
teach.note: Check 8 x 9 x 5 = 360. HCF smaller index, LCM larger index. Ask: how can you tell the answers are sensible (HCF divides both; LCM is a multiple of both)?

practice: Given 36 = 2² x 3² and 48 = 2⁴ x 3, find the HCF and LCM.
Write 28 and 42 as products of primes, then find their HCF and LCM.
Draw a Venn diagram for 12 and 20.
independent: Find the HCF and LCM of: 30 and 42; 54 and 90; 100 and 150.
A = 2³ x 5 x 7 and B = 2² x 3 x 5. Find the HCF and the LCM of A and B, leaving answers in index form.
Two bells ring every 36 s and 48 s. After how many seconds will they next ring together?
Show that 14 is the HCF of 70 and 98 using prime factors.
exit: Find the HCF of 40 and 60 using prime factors.
Find the LCM of 20 and 30 using prime factors.
lessons.homework: Choose two numbers between 50 and 100. Use prime factors to find their HCF and LCM and check your answers.
lessons.send: SEND: Venn diagram templates with prime factors on cards. EAL: pre-teach product/shared/overlap. Stretch: HCF and LCM of three numbers.

lessons.title: Sequences and term-to-term rules
objectives: Describe a sequence using a term-to-term rule
Generate terms from a rule and extend sequences

keywords.def: a list of numbers that follow a rule
one number in a sequence
the rule to get from one term to the next
getting bigger / getting smaller

starter: Say Bismillah. Continue: 5, 10, 15, 20, ...
Work out 3 x 5 + 2.
What is -4 + 7?

teach.heading: What is a sequence?
bullets: A sequence is a list of numbers following a rule.
teach.note: Show patterns from life: days of the week, prayer-time numbers in a day, matchstick patterns. Introduce the words first term, second term and so on.

teach.heading: Term-to-term rules
teach.note: Ask pupils to find the rule by looking at the gap between neighbouring terms. Next terms: 19, 23 / 30, 25 / 162, 486.

teach.heading: Decimals and negatives
teach.note: Continue: next terms 3.3, 4.0 and -6, -10. Make sure pupils can count back through zero.

teach.heading: Two-step rules
bullets: Start at 5. Rule: multiply by 2, then add 1.
teach.note: Next term: 47 x 2 + 1 = 95. Emphasise that the rule is applied to the previous term only.

practice: Write the next two terms and the rule: 8, 14, 20, 26, ...
Write the first four terms: first term 3, rule add 5.
Describe the rule: 81, 27, 9, 3, ...
independent: Find the rule and the next two terms: 7, 13, 19; 100, 90, 80; 1, 4, 16; 0.2, 0.5, 0.8.
Write the first five terms: first term 2, rule multiply by 3 then subtract 1.
A sequence starts 6, 11, 16, 21. Will 100 be in the sequence? Explain.
Write a sequence of your own with a term-to-term rule and give it to a partner.
exit: Write the next two terms: 9, 13, 17, 21, ...
A sequence starts at 4 and the rule is double then subtract 1. Write the first four terms.
lessons.homework: Find three sequences from real life (for example saving £5 each week) and write down their term-to-term rules.
lessons.send: SEND: sequence strips with gaps to fill. EAL: pre-teach term/rule/next. Stretch: write a rule for a sequence that alternates.

lessons.title: Missing terms and special sequences
objectives: Find missing terms in a sequence
Recognise square, cube, triangular and Fibonacci sequences

keywords.def: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25: numbers multiplied by themselves
1, 3, 6, 10, 15: dots that make triangles
each term is the sum of the previous two
the amount between consecutive terms

starter: Say Bismillah. Work out 6², 3³ and 2⁵.
Find the rule: 12, 19, 26, 33.

teach.heading: Missing terms
teach.note: Also try 3, __, 11, __: step = 4, so the missing terms are 7 and 15. Check the pattern works from the start.

teach.heading: Square and cube numbers
teach.note: Draw dot squares. Learn squares to 15² and cubes to 5³ and 10³. Common error: 3² = 6. Differences between consecutive squares are the odd numbers 3, 5, 7, 9.

teach.heading: Triangular and Fibonacci
teach.note: Build triangles with counters. Fibonacci: add the previous two terms. 8 + 13 = 21. Optional: Fibonacci helped spread the Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe through his book Liber Abaci (1202), having learned them from Arabic-speaking mathematicians in North Africa.

teach.heading: Is it in the sequence?
bullets: Is 100 in it? 97 is not a multiple of 4. No.
teach.note: This leads towards the nth term next lesson. Ask: what do all terms have in common? (remainder 3 when divided by 4).

practice: Find the missing terms: 2, __, __, __, 22.
Write the next three triangular numbers after 21.
Is 50 a term in the sequence 6, 11, 16, 21, ...? Explain.
independent: Which of 144, 150, 169 are square numbers? Which are cube numbers? Check 125 and 216.
In the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, ..., will 100 be a term? Will 101?
exit: Find the missing terms: 3, __, __, 18.
Write the first six triangular numbers.
lessons.homework: Draw the first five triangular numbers as dot patterns and find a rule for the differences between terms.
lessons.send: SEND: counters and dot patterns, sequence strips. EAL: pre-teach square/cube/triangular. Stretch: explain why the differences in a square sequence are odd numbers.

lessons.title: Position-to-term rules and the nth term
objectives: Use a position-to-term rule to find terms
Understand the meaning of the nth term

keywords.def: the place of a term in the sequence: 1st, 2nd, 3rd and so on
a formula that gives any term in a sequence from its position n
a sequence with a constant difference between terms

starter: Say Bismillah. Find the rule: 5, 8, 11, 14.
Work out 3 x 7 + 2.
Work out 4 x 10 - 3.

teach.heading: Position and term
bullets: The position n tells us which term.
teach.note: Draw a table: position n in the top row, term in the bottom. Ask why we need a position-to-term rule: to find the 100th term without listing 99 others.

teach.heading: A rule from n
bullets: Rule: 3n + 2 means multiply n by 3, then add 2.
teach.note: Check that the rule matches 8 for n = 2 and 11 for n = 3. Then use n = 10: 3 x 10 + 2 = 32. Stress that the nth term is a formula, not a single number.

teach.heading: Why the number in front of n?
bullets: The sequence goes up by 3 each time.
teach.note: Compare 3, 6, 9, 12 with the sequence 5, 8, 11, 14: each term is 2 more. That 2 is the constant. This sets up the finding method next lesson.

teach.heading: Using the nth term
teach.note: Ask pupils to find the first four terms (3, 7, 11, 15) and the difference (4). Highlight the link between the coefficient of n and the common difference.

practice: The nth term is 2n + 5. Find the first four terms.
The nth term is 5n - 3. Find the 10th term.
The nth term is 3n + 1. Is 40 a term?
independent: Find the first four terms and the 20th term for: 6n; n + 8; 4n - 3; 10 - n.
Find the 50th term of 7n + 2 and of 3n - 4.
The nth term is 6n + 1. Is 85 a term? Is 91?
Write down the nth term of the sequence of multiples of 9.
exit: The nth term is 3n + 4. Find the 5th term.
What is the common difference in the sequence with nth term 7n - 2?
lessons.homework: Choose four different nth term rules, write the first five terms of each, and describe what the number in front of n does.
lessons.send: SEND: position-term table templates. EAL: pre-teach nth term/formula. Stretch: find which term first exceeds 1,000.

lessons.title: Finding the nth term of a linear sequence
objectives: Find the nth term of a linear sequence
Use the nth term to check whether a number is in a sequence

keywords.def: the constant amount added or subtracted between terms
a formula giving the term at position n
the number multiplying a letter, such as 3 in 3n

starter: Say Bismillah. Find the 10th term of 3n - 2.
What is the common difference in 8, 13, 18, 23?
Write the first four multiples of 4.

teach.heading: Step 1: common difference
teach.note: Write the multiples of 4 underneath the sequence. Ask what the difference is between each term and the matching multiple.

teach.heading: Step 2: adjust
teach.note: Check with n = 1: 4 + 3 = 7 and n = 4: 16 + 3 = 19. Always check with at least two terms.

teach.heading: Decreasing sequences
teach.note: Compare the sequence with -3n: 20 - (-3) = 23. Check n = 2: 23 - 6 = 17 and n = 4: 23 - 12 = 11.

teach.heading: Is a number in the sequence?
teach.note: n must be a positive whole number. Also find a term: the 100th term of 3n - 1 is 299.

practice: Find the nth term: 5, 8, 11, 14, ...
Find the nth term: 2, 6, 10, 14, ...
Find the nth term: 30, 26, 22, 18, ...
independent: Is 77 a term in the sequence 5, 12, 19, 26, ...? Show working.
The nth term is 6n - 5. Which term is equal to 115?
Match patterns: matchsticks 4, 7, 10, 13 for 1, 2, 3, 4 squares in a row. Write the nth term and the number of matches for 25 squares.
exit: Find the nth term: 6, 10, 14, 18, ...
Is 52 a term of 3n + 1? Show how you know.
lessons.homework: Make up three linear sequences, one increasing, one decreasing and one with decimals, and find the nth term of each.
lessons.send: SEND: step-by-step frame (difference, multiples, adjust). EAL: model the sentence 'the nth term is'. Stretch: find the nth term of a quadratic sequence like 2, 5, 10, 17.

lessons.title: Perimeter and area of rectangles
objectives: Calculate the perimeter and area of rectangles and squares
Use area and perimeter to find missing lengths

keywords.def: the total distance around the outside of a shape
the amount of surface inside a 2D shape, in square units
the area of a square with sides 1 cm

starter: Say Bismillah. Work out 12 x 7 and 8 x 6.
How many centimetres in a metre?
Draw a rectangle 4 cm by 3 cm. What is its perimeter?

teach.heading: Perimeter
bullets: Add the lengths of all the sides.
12 cm by 7 cm: P = 2 x 19 = 38 cm.
teach.note: Walk the perimeter on a diagram with a finger. Units are cm, m and so on (length). Common error: forgetting two sides.

teach.heading: Area
bullets: Area is measured in square units.
teach.note: Show 12 by 7 squares on squared paper to prove 84. Explain cm²: squares 1 cm by 1 cm. A square of side 9 cm has perimeter 36 cm and area 81 cm².

teach.heading: Working backwards
teach.note: Ask: could another rectangle have the same area but a different perimeter? 9 by 8 gives area 72 and perimeter 34.

teach.heading: Different units
bullets: Room 8 m by 6 m has area 48 m².
Tiles 0.5 m by 0.5 m cover 0.25 m² each.
teach.note: 48 ÷ 0.25 = 192 tiles. Context: carpeting a prayer room or tiling a school corridor. Ask why the units must match before multiplying.

practice: A rectangle is 15 cm by 8 cm. Find its perimeter and area.
A square has perimeter 44 cm. Find its side and area.
A rectangle has area 54 cm² and width 6 cm. Find its length and perimeter.
independent: Find the perimeter and area: 9 m by 4 m; 2.5 cm by 6 cm; 13 mm by 20 mm.
A playground is 40 m by 25 m. A fence goes round it. How long is the fence? What is the area?
A rectangle has perimeter 30 cm and one side 9 cm. Find the other side and the area.
A prayer hall is 12 m by 8 m. Carpet tiles are 0.5 m by 0.5 m. How many tiles are needed?
exit: Find the perimeter and area of a rectangle 11 cm by 6 cm.
A rectangle has area 60 cm² and length 12 cm. What is its width?
lessons.homework: Measure the length and width of two rectangular things at home (a table, a door). Calculate their perimeter and area.
lessons.send: SEND: squared paper, counting squares first. EAL: pre-teach perimeter/area with diagrams. Stretch: find all rectangles with whole-number sides and area 36 cm² and compare their perimeters.

lessons.title: Compound shapes
objectives: Find the area and perimeter of compound shapes made from rectangles
Choose an efficient way to split a shape

keywords.def: a shape made by joining simpler shapes
made up of several parts
a compound shape made from two rectangles

starter: Say Bismillah. A rectangle is 14 cm by 5 cm. Find the area.
What is the perimeter of a square with side 8 cm?
Find the missing side: area 48 cm², length 8 cm.

teach.heading: Split into rectangles
bullets: Draw a line to split the shape into rectangles.
Write down any missing side lengths first.
teach.note: Pupils label every side before calculating. Missing lengths are found by adding or subtracting known sides on the opposite edge.

teach.heading: Worked L-shape
bullets: Bottom rectangle: 12 cm by 4 cm = 48 cm².
Top block: 5 cm by 6 cm = 30 cm².
teach.note: Shape: the bottom rectangle is 12 wide and 4 tall; the top block is 5 wide and 6 tall, sitting on the left. Total height is 10 cm. Show alternative splits to confirm: left strip 5 by 10 = 50, right strip 7 by 4 = 28, total 78.

teach.heading: Perimeter of the L-shape
bullets: Right side 4 cm, step in 7 cm.
Then 6 cm up, 5 cm across, 10 cm down.
teach.note: Notice 44 = 2(12 + 10): the perimeter equals that of the bounding rectangle when the missing piece is a corner. Pupils should work out the missing side 12 - 5 = 7 first.

teach.heading: Subtracting a corner
bullets: Big rectangle 10 cm by 8 cm = 80 cm².
Cut-out corner 4 cm by 3 cm = 12 cm².
teach.note: Compare adding pieces and subtracting a piece. The cut-out method is often quicker. Perimeter of this shape is still 2(10 + 8) = 36 cm.

practice: An L-shape is made from a 9 cm by 3 cm rectangle and a 4 cm by 5 cm rectangle joined. Find the area.
A 14 cm by 10 cm rectangle has a 5 cm by 4 cm corner removed. Find the area.
Find the perimeter of the shape in question 2.
independent: An L-shape has outer lengths 15 cm and 11 cm. The cut-out corner is 6 cm by 5 cm. Find its area and perimeter.
A garden is 20 m by 12 m with a 6 m by 4 m patio in one corner. Find the area of grass.
A T-shape is made of a 10 cm by 3 cm bar and a 3 cm by 7 cm stem below the middle. Find its area.
A school floor plan is two rectangles, 8 m by 5 m and 6 m by 4 m. Find the total floor area and the paint needed at 1 litre per 6 m² (round up).
exit: Find the area of an L-shape made of a 10 cm by 2 cm and a 3 cm by 5 cm rectangle.
A 12 cm by 9 cm rectangle has a 4 cm by 3 cm corner removed. What is the area?
lessons.homework: Sketch an L-shaped room (a classroom, a garden) and measure or estimate its area and perimeter.
lessons.send: SEND: shapes on squared paper to cut and split; label sides first. EAL: pre-teach compound/split. Stretch: shapes with a notch in the middle of a side.

lessons.title: Area of a triangle
objectives: Use the formula A = ½ x base x height for a triangle
Find a missing base or height

keywords.def: the side of a triangle used to measure its height from
the height measured at a right angle to the base
the longest side of a right-angled triangle

starter: Say Bismillah. What is half of 36?
Find the area of a 9 cm by 6 cm rectangle.
What do we call an angle of 90 degrees?

teach.heading: Half a rectangle
bullets: A right-angled triangle is half a rectangle.
Rectangle 10 cm by 6 cm has area 60 cm².
teach.note: Draw a rectangle and its diagonal. Cut and show two congruent triangles. Extend to any triangle by drawing its perpendicular height.

teach.heading: The formula
bullets: Area = ½ x base x perpendicular height.
Base 10, height 6: A = ½ x 10 x 6 = 30 cm².
Use the height at right angles to the base.
teach.note: The slanted side is not the height unless the triangle is right-angled at the base. Common error: using the sloping side. Show an obtuse and an acute triangle with the height marked.

teach.heading: Examples
bullets: Base 9, height 8: A = ½ x 9 x 8 = 36 cm².
Base 7.5 cm, height 4 cm: A = 15 cm².
5-12-13 triangle: A = ½ x 5 x 12 = 30 cm².
teach.note: In the 5-12-13 right-angled triangle, the 5 and 12 are perpendicular, so use them as base and height. The 13 is the hypotenuse and is not used.

teach.heading: Working backwards
teach.note: Alternative: double the area (48) and divide by the base (8). Check: ½ x 8 x 6 = 24.

practice: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 5 cm.
A triangle has area 35 cm² and base 10 cm. Find its height.
A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm and hypotenuse 10 cm. Find its area.
independent: Find the area: base 14 cm, height 9 cm; base 6.4 cm, height 5 cm; base 3 m, height 2.5 m.
A triangular flag has base 80 cm and height 50 cm. Find its area.
A triangle has area 48 cm² and height 8 cm. Find the base.
A rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm has one corner cut off along a diagonal. Find the area of the triangle that remains and the area cut off.
exit: Find the area of a triangle with base 16 cm and height 7 cm.
A triangle has area 20 cm² and height 5 cm. Find its base.
lessons.homework: Draw three different triangles on squared paper. Measure the base and height of each and calculate the area.
lessons.send: SEND: triangles on squared paper with height drawn; cut-out rectangle to show half. EAL: pre-teach base/height/perpendicular. Stretch: composite shapes with triangles.

lessons.title: Area of a parallelogram
objectives: Use the formula A = base x perpendicular height for a parallelogram
Distinguish perpendicular height from the slant side

keywords.def: a four-sided shape with two pairs of parallel sides
the height measured at a right angle to the base
the sloping side, which is not the height

starter: Say Bismillah. Find the area of a triangle with base 8 cm and height 5 cm.
What is the area of a rectangle 7 cm by 6 cm?
Name two properties of a parallelogram.

teach.heading: Turn it into a rectangle
bullets: Cut a right-angled triangle from one end.
Move it to the other end.
teach.note: Demonstrate with paper: cut and slide. The base and perpendicular height stay the same, so the area is unchanged.

teach.heading: The formula
bullets: Base 9 cm, height 5 cm: A = 45 cm².
The slant side of 6 cm is not used.
teach.note: Show a diagram with a dotted height. Common error: multiplying base by slant side (9 x 6 = 54). Ask why that is not the area.

teach.heading: Missing lengths
teach.note: Practise rearranging. Link to the triangle: a triangle on the same base and height has half the area.

teach.heading: Parallelogram or triangle?
bullets: Triangle: ½ x base x height.
teach.note: Give a quick quiz: show shapes and ask which formula applies. Finish with a compound shape: parallelogram 10 by 4 plus triangle with base 10 and height 3 on top: 40 + 15 = 55.

practice: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 12 cm and height 7 cm.
A parallelogram has area 63 cm² and height 9 cm. Find its base.
A parallelogram has sides 10 cm and 6 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm to the 10 cm base. Find its area.
independent: Find the area: base 15 cm, height 8 cm; base 4.5 m, height 3 m; base 20 mm, height 13 mm.
A parallelogram has area 96 cm² and base 12 cm. Find its height.
A tile is a parallelogram with base 24 cm and height 10 cm. How many tiles cover 2.4 m²? (1 m² = 10,000 cm²)
Find the area of a shape made from a parallelogram (base 10 cm, height 4 cm) with a triangle (base 10 cm, height 3 cm) on top.
exit: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 14 cm and height 6 cm.
Explain why we do not use the slant side when finding area.
lessons.homework: Draw two different parallelograms with the same base and height on squared paper. Show they have the same area.
lessons.send: SEND: paper cut-outs to rearrange; squared paper. EAL: pre-teach parallel/perpendicular. Stretch: prove the triangle formula from the parallelogram formula.

lessons.title: Area of a trapezium
objectives: Use the formula A = ½(a + b)h for a trapezium
Find a missing length from the area

keywords.def: a four-sided shape with one pair of parallel sides
sides that stay the same distance apart
the distance between the parallel sides at right angles

starter: Say Bismillah. Work out ½ x (6 + 10) x 4.
Find the area of a parallelogram with base 8 cm and height 5 cm.
Find the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 4 cm.

teach.heading: Two copies make a parallelogram
bullets: Rotate a copy of the trapezium and join it.
The base is a + b; the height is h.
teach.note: Demonstrate with paper trapezia. The trapezium is half of the parallelogram, which gives the formula.

teach.heading: The formula
bullets: Area = ½ x (a + b) x h.
a and b are the parallel sides.
h is the perpendicular height between them.
teach.note: Common errors: using the slant side as h, or forgetting the half. Mark a, b and h in different colours.

teach.heading: Worked examples
bullets: Sides 6, 10, height 4: A = ½ x 16 x 4 = 32.
Sides 8, 14, height 5: A = ½ x 22 x 5 = 55.
teach.note: Show the working in lines: add the parallel sides, halve, then multiply by the height. 22 ÷ 2 = 11, 11 x 5 = 55.

teach.heading: Missing height
teach.note: Check: ½ x (7 + 11) x 6 = 9 x 6 = 54. Ask pupils to create their own trapezium with area 40 cm².

practice: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and height 6 cm.
Find the area with parallel sides 12 cm and 18 cm and height 10 cm.
A trapezium has area 48 cm², parallel sides 5 cm and 7 cm. Find its height.
independent: Find the area: sides 4 and 10, height 5; sides 9 and 15, height 8; sides 3.5 and 6.5, height 4.
A field is a trapezium with parallel sides 60 m and 100 m and distance 40 m between them. Find its area.
A trapezium has area 70 cm² and height 7 cm. One parallel side is 6 cm. Find the other.
Choose the correct formula and find each area: rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm; triangle base 10 cm, height 6 cm; parallelogram base 7 cm, height 5 cm; trapezium sides 4 cm and 8 cm, height 3 cm.
exit: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 8 cm and 12 cm and height 5 cm.
A trapezium has area 36 cm² and height 4 cm. The sum of the parallel sides is?
lessons.homework: Find a trapezium in the real world (a bag, a table end, a roof) and estimate its area using the formula.
lessons.send: SEND: formula cards with colour-coded a, b and h. EAL: pre-teach trapezium/parallel. Stretch: split a trapezium into a rectangle and two triangles and verify the formula.

lessons.title: The number line, ordering and adding with negatives
objectives: Order positive and negative numbers using inequality symbols
Add and subtract positive numbers from negative numbers

keywords.def: a number less than zero
a statement using < or > to compare numbers
a number with a positive or negative sign

starter: Say Bismillah. Which is colder: -6 degrees or -2 degrees?
Work out 5 - 8.
Order smallest first: 3, -1, 0, -7.

teach.heading: Ordering negatives
bullets: The further left on the number line, the smaller.
teach.note: Draw the number line from -10 to 10. Misconception: -10 is bigger than -2 because 10 > 2. Use temperatures or debts: owing £10 is worse than owing £2.

teach.heading: Adding positives
bullets: Move right on the number line.
teach.note: Count on from the negative number: -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. For -7 + 4 we land at -3, still negative. Use a thermometer to model.

teach.heading: Subtracting positives
bullets: Move left on the number line.
teach.note: Subtracting makes the number smaller. Use a bank account balance: balance -£40 and a payment of £25 makes -£65, and a deposit of £25 makes -£15.

teach.heading: Contexts
bullets: Lift at floor -2 goes up 6: floor 4.
teach.note: Ask pupils to write the calculation each time: -40 + 25 = -15; -2 + 6 = 4; 3 - 8 = -5. Stress saying the calculation in words.

practice: Put in order, smallest first: 5, -8, 0, -3, 2, -6.
The temperature is -4 degrees and rises by 11 degrees. What is it now?
independent: A submarine is at -120 m, rises 45 m, then dives 70 m. Where is it now?
Find the missing numbers: -5 + ? = 8; 3 - ? = -4; ? + 9 = 2.
exit: Work out -6 + 10 and 4 - 9.
lessons.homework: Record the overnight temperatures for a week using a weather website (some places will be negative) and order them.
lessons.send: SEND: number line on desk, counters for jumps. EAL: pre-teach negative/rise/fall. Stretch: add and subtract decimals such as -2.5 + 1.75.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting negative numbers
objectives: Add and subtract negative numbers
Explain the rule for subtracting a negative

keywords.def: less than zero
two minus signs in a row, which make a plus
a +1 and -1 together, which make 0

starter: Say Bismillah. Work out -3 + 8 and 4 - 9.
Work out 7 - 7.

teach.heading: Adding a negative
bullets: It has the same effect as 3 - 5.
teach.note: Think of debts: if you have £3 and then take on a debt of £5, you are £2 in debt. Draw the number line: add a negative means move left.

teach.heading: Subtracting a negative
bullets: 5 - (-3) means take away a debt of 3.
Taking away a negative makes you better off.
teach.note: Use zero pairs with counters: to take away -3 from 5, add zero pairs until three negatives can be removed. Or temperature difference: from -3 up to 5 is 8 degrees.

teach.heading: The signs rule
bullets: Two same signs in a row make +.
Two different signs in a row make -.
teach.note: Examples: -4 - (-6) = -4 + 6 = 2; 3 + (-5) = -2; -2 - (-2) = 0. Ask pupils to describe each step in words.

teach.heading: Temperature difference
teach.note: Link to the distance across zero from last year. Both methods give 12. Ask: why do we get a bigger answer when subtracting a negative?

practice: Work out 6 + (-2) and 6 - (-2).
Work out -4 - (-9).
Work out -3 + (-5).
independent: Highest 9 degrees and lowest -13 degrees. Find the difference.
exit: Work out 3 - (-7).
Work out -5 + (-4).
lessons.homework: Write six calculations with double signs, such as 7 - (-2), solve them and describe each in words.
lessons.send: SEND: coloured counters for positive and negative; zero pairs. EAL: say 'minus negative'. Stretch: decimals and fractions.

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing negative numbers
objectives: Multiply and divide positive and negative numbers
Carry out mixed calculations with negatives

keywords.def: the result of a multiplication
the result of a division
two numbers with the same sign (both + or both -)
two numbers with different signs

starter: Say Bismillah. Work out 5 - (-2) and -6 + (-3).
Work out 3 x 4 and 12 ÷ 3.
Continue the pattern: 3 x 2 = 6, 2 x 2 = 4, 1 x 2 = 2, 0 x 2 = ...

teach.heading: A pattern to follow
teach.note: Each step the answer goes up by 2. Continue: (-2) x (-2) = 4. This convinces pupils that two negatives give a positive, not just a rule to memorise.

teach.heading: The rule for multiplying
bullets: Like signs give a positive answer.
Unlike signs give a negative answer.
teach.note: Check -3 x 4 as repeated addition: -3 + -3 + -3 + -3 = -12. Summary: positive x positive = positive; negative x negative = positive; mixed = negative.

teach.heading: Dividing the same way
bullets: Division follows the same sign rule.
teach.note: Link to multiplication: -4 x -5 = 20 so 20 ÷ (-5) = -4. Missing number: ? x (-4) = 28 gives ? = -7.

teach.heading: Mixed calculations
teach.note: Common error: thinking (-3) x (-3) is -9. Like signs give a positive, so it is 9.

practice: Find the missing number: ? x (-6) = 42.
independent: Fill in the missing numbers: (-5) x ? = 35; ? ÷ (-4) = -9; (-3) x ? = -27.
Explain in your own words why (-3) x (-4) = 12, using a pattern.
exit: Work out (-6) x (-7) and (-48) ÷ 8.
Work out (-2) x 9 + 3.
lessons.homework: Make a one-page summary of the sign rules for all four operations with a worked example of each.
lessons.send: SEND: sign-rule card and the multiplication pattern table. EAL: say 'negative times negative equals positive' together. Stretch: powers of negative numbers such as (-2)³.
